title: One password, multiple accounts — question explanation
learningObjective: Avoid password reuse across services and understand credential-stuffing exposure
format: 16:9 educational motion-graphics video; narration; separate captions; no autoplay with sound
visualStyle: Deep navy and charcoal; restrained cyan/electric-blue highlights; limited purple accents; clean typography; purposeful, low-motion transitions; accessible contrast.

scenes.name: Scenario setup
scenes.visual: You use the same password for a shopping site and your school account. The shopping site reports a data breach.
scenes.direction: Show a fictional simulated setting. Use generic UI and no actual organization, brand, user identity, credential, real URL or live account.

scenes.name: Learning objective and risk cue
scenes.visual: Avoid password reuse across services and understand credential-stuffing exposure
scenes.direction: Highlight only observable cues and explain the decision context without implying certainty beyond the scenario.

scenes.name: Recommended response
scenes.visual: Option C: Change the reused password to a unique one and review other accounts where it was reused. A breach at one service can expose a password reused elsewhere; unique credentials limit cross-service compromise.
scenes.direction: Animate the recommended defensive choice as a clear decision path. Display the action verb and trusted channel/control.

scenes.name: Why the other options fail
scenes.visual: Option A: Waiting leaves an exposed credential in use; address the reuse promptly. Option B: MFA adds protection but does not make password reuse safe; stolen credentials can still be abused. Option D: A predictable minor variation still preserves password reuse and may be guessable.
scenes.direction: Show each unsafe alternative separately with a complete, concise reason. Do not depict operational exploitation, malicious code or credential capture.

scenes.name: Defensive takeaway
scenes.visual: Change the school password to a unique strong password, change other reused instances, and check account activity. Use a unique password for every account so one service’s breach does not unlock another.
scenes.direction: Close with one readable takeaway and the next safe action. Keep the final frame long enough for comprehension.
scenes.onScreenText: Use a unique password for every account so one service’s breach does not unlock another.

narration: Scenario: You use the same password for a shopping site and your school account. The shopping site reports a data breach. Safest response: Option C: Change the reused password to a unique one and review other accounts where it was reused. A breach at one service can expose a password reused elsewhere; unique credentials limit cross-service compromise. Option A is unsafe because Waiting leaves an exposed credential in use; address the reuse promptly. Option B is unsafe because MFA adds protection but does not make password reuse safe; stolen credentials can still be abused. Option D is unsafe because A predictable minor variation still preserves password reuse and may be guessable. In practice: Change the school password to a unique strong password, change other reused instances, and check account activity. Key takeaway: Use a unique password for every account so one service’s breach does not unlock another.
